opus-5.5.text:
That's a great question, and honestly it's one we think about every single day.

The way I look at it, there are a few layers to "readiness." The first is visual quality: does the model look good enough at first glance? A couple of years ago the answer was usually no. You'd get blobby shapes and muddy textures. Today, for a lot of categories like props, environment pieces, and stylized characters, the first impression is often good enough.

But game studios don't ship first impressions. They ship assets that have to work inside an engine, under real constraints. So the second layer is production readiness. Is the topology clean? Is the polycount reasonable for the target platform? Are the UVs laid out sensibly? Do you get proper PBR materials, so the asset looks right under the game's lighting and not just in a pretty preview render? For characters, can it be rigged and animated without an artist spending two days fixing it? This is where the gap between "demo-ready" and "production-ready" really shows up.

The third layer, which people often overlook, is workflow fit. Even a technically perfect asset isn't useful if it doesn't match the art direction, or if the artist can't easily iterate on it. Studios need control: consistent style, the ability to edit, export to the formats and pipelines they already use, whether that's Unity, Unreal, Blender, or something in-house.

So in practice, the most honest metric I use is how much human time it saves end to end. If an artist takes an AI-generated model and spends 20 minutes cleaning it up instead of building it from scratch over a day or two, that's a real win, even if the asset isn't perfect out of the box. Today we're clearly there for background assets, prototyping, and indie teams moving fast. For hero assets, like a main character in a AAA game, AI is more of a starting point or a concept tool, and a skilled artist is still essential.

My view is that it's not a binary "ready or not ready." It's a moving frontier, and it moves very quickly. Every few months, a category of assets crosses the line from "nice demo" to "people are actually shipping this." Our job is to keep pushing that line, while listening very closely to what artists tell us breaks in their pipeline.

r001.rationale: The response describes a gap between demo and production readiness, says artists may need to clean up generated models, and notes that hero assets still require skilled artists.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd say we're at an interesting inflection point, and the honest answer depends a lot on what you mean by "ready."

If you ask whether a studio can type a prompt and drop the output straight into a shipping AAA title, we're not there yet. The core problem is that a game asset isn't just a shape that looks right from one angle. It needs clean topology so it deforms properly when animated, sensible UV layouts so the textures don't stretch, correct polygon budgets for the target platform, and PBR materials that behave consistently under the game's lighting. A lot of generated meshes today still look great in a turntable render and then fall apart the moment a rigger or a technical artist opens them. You get self-intersecting geometry, baked-in lighting that fights the engine, and surfaces that need a lot of retopology before anyone can touch them.

That said, I think the "not ready" framing misses where the real value already is. Studios are using these tools very effectively for ideation, for blocking out environments, for background props, for the long tail of assets that nobody wants to spend an artist's week on. If you need two hundred variations of crates, rocks, and street furniture to fill out a level, generation plus a quick cleanup pass is already faster than modeling from scratch. The economics shift the moment the output is "good enough to edit" rather than "good enough to ship untouched." And the key is that the human in the loop moves up the stack. Artists spend less time on the mechanical parts and more time on art direction and polish.

The other thing I'd flag is that the quality ceiling is moving quickly. A year or two ago the geometry was the bottleneck. Now the geometry is often fine and the conversation has shifted to materials, to consistency across a set of assets, to controllability. Can I say "make this one match that one's style"? Can I get a mesh with a specific triangle count? Those are the questions studios actually ask, and they're much more tractable engineering problems than "can a model hallucinate a plausible chair."

So my assessment is this: ready for pre-production, ready for background and filler content, increasingly ready for hero assets with a human finishing pass, and not yet ready as a replacement for a skilled 3D artist on anything a player stares at for more than a second. But the gap is closing faster than most people in the industry expected, and I think the studios that will benefit most are the ones building pipelines now, with the assumption that the quality will keep improving underneath them.

r001.rationale: The response says generated meshes often need a quick cleanup pass or substantial retopology, and describes hero assets as increasingly usable with a human finishing pass.

astra-6.text:
I think it depends on what you mean by ready. If you mean generating something that looks impressive in a demo, we're already seeing that. If you mean an asset that a studio can drop directly into a shipping game, that's a much higher bar.

A game asset needs more than the right appearance. It needs usable geometry, textures, and a structure that fits the studio's workflow. If it's a character, it also needs to deform properly when animated. And all of that has to work within the game's performance budget.

So I would assess readiness by how much work remains after generation. Does it actually save an artist time once you include cleanup and integration? For prototyping or some background objects, the answer can be yes. For a main character with very specific artistic requirements, I would be more cautious. I see the near-term value as helping artists iterate faster, with artists still guiding and validating the result.

r001.rationale: The response says studio-ready assets face a higher bar and assesses readiness by the cleanup and integration work remaining after generation, with artists still guiding and validating results.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it depends on what you mean by “ready.” For prototyping, AI-generated 3D models can already be useful. You can explore an idea quickly, put something into a scene, and see whether it works. But a model that looks good in a preview is different from an asset a studio can ship.

For production, you need to consider topology, UVs, materials, polygon budgets, and whether the asset can be rigged and animated. It also needs to match the art direction and fit into the studio’s existing workflow. Those requirements vary a lot between a background prop and a main character.

So I would think of readiness asset by asset. The practical question is how much work an artist needs to do after generation. If generating and cleaning up an asset takes less time than making it from scratch, while meeting the same quality bar, then it’s useful. That’s a more meaningful benchmark than how impressive a single generated image looks.

r001.rationale: The response says production assets must meet topology, UV, material, rigging, art-direction, and workflow requirements, and frames readiness by the artist’s cleanup work after generation. This clearly communicates that generated models need refinement to meet studio needs.
